Péter Magyar’s pre- and post-election tirades against the cost of the modernization of Hungary’s Paks nuclear power plants, and his suggestions of an alleged plot by the former Orbán government to subordinate the country’s energy sovereignty to the Kremlin, are now coming under increasing scrutiny. Modernizing the Russian-built plant is very expensive indeed, but it is dwarfed by the consequences of not having it, writes the Russian outlet, Ria Novosti.
No sooner has Péter Magyar had a chance to fully savor his election victory than reality brought him crashing back down to earth. On his official page, the new Hungarian prime minister announced a declaration of a state of emergency in the energy sector, wrote the Russian news portal. The national operator MVM Paks Nuclear Power Station is about to shut down the country’s only nuclear power plant, and the decision is in no way related to scheduled preventive maintenance. Energy officials simply have no other choice, as the water level of the Danube—whose waters are used as a natural coolant—has dropped to critically low levels.
The shutdown of four VVER-440 reactors means that 2,000 megawatt-hours of electricity—or 40% of the country’s generation capacity—will be lost from the domestic grid. The head of state is urging his fellow citizens to voluntarily minimize consumption. The Hungarians are not alone in facing problems caused by the summer heatwave. The low water levels in the Danube forced Romania’s Nuclearelectrica to shut down the first power unit at the Cernavodă Nuclear Power Plant last Wednesday, and two days later, the second reactor suffered the same fate.
To understand the essence of what is happening, it should be noted that the core cooling systems of nuclear power plants can be configured in two ways, write Ria Novosti.
The simplest method is the direct flow method. Water from a river, lake, or the sea is piped to the turbine condensers, where it absorbs excess heat, and then, having been heated, is returned to the source. This method is the most reliable, but it requires a truly enormous amount of water. Depending on the turbines’ capacity, the flow rate can range from forty to one hundred cubic meters per second; accordingly, over 250 million cubic meters of water pass through the plant each month.
